content.title: The Most Memorable Celebrity Covers of JFK Jr.'s 'George' Magazine
content.text: When John F. Kennedy Jr. co-founded a political magazine in 1995, nobody knew how it would be received. Marrying current affairs and pop culture with the tagline "not just politics as usual," George was a creative risk — yet immediately after launching with supermodel Cindy Crawford on the cover, it made a splash. "I recognized not only the reader appeal, but also the advertiser interest it would generate," David Pecker, the then-Hachette publishing CEO, said in an oral history of George published by The Hollywood Reporter. "The first issue sold out with hundreds of ad pages, more than the September issue of Vogue at the time." JFK Jr. stands beside copies of 'George' at the opening of Hudson News in Grand Central Station. Lawrence Schwartzwald/Sygma via Getty In the years that followed, Kennedy's magazine enlisted several other A-listers to grace its cover, often depicting the most topical actors and athletes of the moment in some sort of unusual historic getup that would — in today's world — break the internet. "It was a great concept ahead of its time," Jack Kliger, another former Hachette executive, told Esquire in 2019. "I wish we would have been able to stick with it because I think it would be a very relevant and needed product today. I think the times have come to George.” Though the monthly magazine faced its share of financial difficulties over the years, ultimately shuttering two years after Kennedy's death, in 2001, it produced countless iconic images of the era's biggest stars and most promising up-and-comers across its 57 issues. Below, some of the most memorable celebrity covers of George published between 1995 and 2001. Cindy Crawford Cindy Crawford. Issue: October/November 1995 The iconic inaugural George cover featuring Cindy Crawford as sexy George Washington kicked off the magazine's run with a hit — and Carolyn Bessette may be the person to thank. "We had dinner in Tribeca; [photographer] Herb Ritts, me, John and Carolyn. We needed to figure out what the first cover would be," creative director Matt Berman recalled to The Hollywood Reporter. "We started throwing out names, lots of them. Everybody who was anybody. All women. When Cindy’s name came up, Carolyn butted in and said, 'That is perfect. She is apple pie. All-American. Self-made. She’s it.' Herb called Cindy from the restaurant." After Ryan Murphy's Love Story premiered on FX in February 2026, Crawford reposted scenes from her cover shoot on Instagram, writing, "Taking a trip down memory lane with @lovestoryfx…" Robert De Niro Robert De Niro. Issue: December 1995/January 1996 The second cover of George reprised the depiction of George Washington, this time with Robert De Niro reportedly holding Washington's real sword that had been gifted to President John F. Kennedy. Reflecting on how the photoshoot came to fruition, De Niro — who was promoting Heat and Casino at the time — told THR, "We might have talked about it at Bubby’s [a Tribeca restaurant John frequented]. I just did it, you know?" Charles Barkley Charles Barkley. Issue: February/March 1996 NBA legend Charles Barkley was seriously considering a future in politics in the '90s when he got a call from Kennedy asking to be interviewed for George. "I said no to his interview request," Barkley told Sports Illustrated in 2015. "But then all the girls from the Suns said, 'Hey, we need to talk to you?' I said, 'About what?' They said, 'You are doing this interview no matter what!' It was so funny." Demi Moore Demi Moore. Issue: June/July 1996 Timed with the release of her comedy-thriller Striptease, Demi Moore dressed in a colorful colonial getup — this time depicting first lady Martha Washington, with her bare skin painted in red and white stripes and her hands on the strings of a George Washington puppet. “She was at the height of her fame, and she was really involved in the cover, calling my office a million times, going over everything,” Berman told Vanity Fair. According to Berman, Moore wasn't happy with the final photo, but when Berman assured her that Kennedy loved it and said he'd feel disappointed to hear her complaints, she reportedly backpedaled. Drew Barrymore Drew Barrymore. Issue: September 1996 Drew Barrymore's George cover was easily the most controversial, nodding to Marilyn Monroe's infamous 1962 performance for President John F. Kennedy, which sparked affair rumors. Barrymore recalled on her talk show that when she found out the theme of the photoshoot, she said, "Oh, okay... I'd really love some direction from you on what the tone is." "[Kennedy] just said, 'I want it to be straightforward. I don't want it to be buffoonery. I don't want it to be over congratulatory. I want it to be this sort of sensual, straightforward, confident moment,' " Barrymore said. "And then we went and did the shoot and I heard they were really happy with the pictures and that was great. And then I saw the magazine and I was like, 'Oh my God, this is so crazy,' " she added of the photos by Mario Sorrenti. Barbra Streisand Barbra Streisand. Issue: November 1996 Berman wrote a lengthy story for Vanity Fair in 2014 about his nerve-racking experience working with Barbra Streisand for a cover, after Carolyn allegedly warned him, "She’ll eat you alive." Berman and Kennedy took a trip out to her L.A. home to meet her and — moments after she finished a separate shoot for InStyle — they got the photos they needed of Streisand as Betsy Ross, the mother of the American flag. Woody Harrelson Woody Harrelson. Issue: December 1996 Woody Harrelson dressed down and threw on some angel wings to grace the cover of George's "What Does America Believe?" issue, which featured an exclusive interview with then-President Bill Clinton. At the time, Harrelson's movie The People vs. Larry Flynt, for which he received an Oscar nomination, was hitting theaters. Claudia Schiffer Claudia Schiffer. Issue: January 1997 German model Claudia Schiffer was honored with bringing one of Berman's early cover ideas to life, posing nude as President Clinton's second term began with only a "Clinton Gore" sash across her body. Karen Mulder Karen Mulder. Issue: February 1997 The February 1997 George issue has become the subject of QAnon conspiracy theories over its interview with Bill Gates, making it one of the most expensive and sought-after covers on eBay. When Berman learned that some people have sought to find "all these hidden meanings" in the cover, he took to Instagram to explain that, in reality, the photoshoot with Dutch model Karen Mulder was the product of thinking outside the box on month when they didn't have a movie star lined up. "John said, 'Maestro, come on, come up with something creative. It can be anything,' " Berman recalled, leading to what he describes as a random "Planet of the Apes meets outer space meets the future meets George magazine" design, complete with George Washington's bust on Mount Rushmore sinking into the ground. Julia Roberts Julia Roberts Issue: March 1997 Movie star Julia Roberts was chosen to portray Susan B. Anthony for George's 1997 "Special Hollywood Issue," ahead of the release of her films My Best Friend's Wedding and Conspiracy Theory. Her portrait was stamped onto a dollar coin in place of the real-life suffragette, creating one of the more memorable issues in the magazine's limited run. Katie Couric Katie Couric. Issue: May 1997 Katie Couric — the longtime Today show star who would go on to host Kennedy's final TV interview before his plane crash in 1999 — was chosen to be the face of a media-themed issue in the spring of 1997. She later reflected that she "had a crush on" Kennedy in the height of his fame and "was so thrilled" to get the honor of gracing his magazine, writing in February 2026, "I have a huge poster of that cover in my basement. Sometimes I look at it, and it feels like a lifetime ago — when my hair was very, very brown." George Clooney George Clooney. Issue: June 1997 George Clooney dressed in his Thomas Jefferson best, holding a copy of the Declaration of Independence, for a 1997 George issue aligned with his debut as Batman. As a leading man in the years since, Clooney has become a prominent Hollywood voice for the Democratic Party. Jenny McCarthy Jenny McCarthy. Issue: July 1997 Jenny McCarthy's trippy George issue captured attention with her American flag tongue, accompanied by an interview where she spoke about fellow Playboy cover star Pamela Anderson and then-Russian President Boris Yeltsin. Harrison Ford Harrison Ford. Issue: August 1997 Harrison Ford was a natural choice for the August 1997 issue of George, on the heels of playing both a fictional U.S. president in Air Force One and an Irish-American police sergeant who gets caught up in an Irish Republican Army plot in The Devil's Own. Ford dressed as Abraham Lincoln for the shoot, and the issue featured an interview with a prominent Irish politician about a ceasefire involving the Irish Republican Army. Kate Moss Kate Moss. Issue: September 1997 Kate Moss' nude cover as the biblical first woman, Eve, came together in an unexpected way, Berman told PEOPLE in an episode of The Trackdown. The cover was initially supposed to feature Pamela Anderson, who pulled out at the last second. "I really didn't know what to do, so I was thinking, 'I better think of something before I call John,' " Berman recalled. "So I spoke to the photographer, who was friends with Kate Moss, so she said, 'Yes, she'll do it.' And I was like, 'Oh, phew.' " Moss' shoot was accompanied by a shirtless photo of Kennedy inside, in a nod to Eve's counterpart, Adam. Elizabeth Hurley Elizabeth Hurley. Issue: October 1997 Austin Power star Elizabeth Hurley nodded to her film's vintage spy look for the "Spy Issue" of George, which explored the real-world intelligence community. Pamela Anderson Pamela Anderson. Issue: January 1998 Only a few months after Kate Moss stepped in for Pamela Anderson on the iconic Eve cover shoot, Kennedy secured Anderson to cover a lookback issue of 1997 politics instead. Anderson later recalled the experience in a poem: Pamela Anderson John F Kennedy Jrcalled me to be on his GEORGE magazine coverWrapped in an American flagHe called me on set.I was nervousI giggled unrecognizably,It was terrible.I couldn’t speak.He was so charming.I couldn’t breatheThis was mymost embarrassing moment. —Pamela Anderson Johnny Depp Johnny Depp. Issue: June 1998 A promo for Johnny Depp's Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas collided with a George issue about the "most fascinating men in politics," including Bill Clinton, Ronald Reagan and Bill Gates. Bruce Willis Bruce Willis. Issue: July 1998 Bruce Willis, at the time an outspoken critic of President Clinton, shared his thoughts on Hollywood Democrats for the 1998 summer issue of George, posing under a tented American flag. His NASA action film Armageddon, released that month, was the highest-grossing film of the year. Charlize Theron Charlize Theron. Issue: August 1998 Berman credits Kennedy with helping to make Charlize Theron a household name years before her Oscar-winning role in Monster. Berman told Page Six in 2014 that after featuring a handful of A-listers in previous covers, “he wanted something unusual that people hadn’t seen before." To bring his vision to life with a lesser-known star, he got in touch with a Miramax executive who recommended "this beautiful model" — Theron. "We picked Charlize up at her apartment. This fun girl just jumps in the van ... we drove to Central Park [and shot her] as ‘sexy Martha Washington,' " Berman recalled. "John just knew all these people. He was really ahead of his time.” Salma Hayek Salma Hayek. Issue: July 1999 Salma Hayek's electric George cover story, titled "Mexican Firecracker" (the inside photos featured her riding a larger-than-life firework), stuck to the theme of her summer blockbuster Wild Wild West. Hayek celebrated the 4th of July in 2024 with an Instagram "#tbt" to the playful shoot, referencing the cover line "Latin Heat." Hayek's issue reached newsstands on the month of Kennedy's tragic death in a plane crash near Martha's Vineyard. Though George continued publishing for two more years, it entered a new era after her cover — one without its visionary editor-in-chief. Arnold Schwarzenegger Arnold Schwarzenegger. Issue: November 1999 After Kennedy's death, George churned out a few more covers with memorable visuals, including one that previewed Arnold Schwarzenegger's 21st-century pivot from Hollywood to government, titled, "Terminator 2000: Arnold's Plan to Fix America." Schwarzenegger — dressed on the cover as a Founding Father on a Terminator 2-inspired motorcycle — would go on to bring his conservative vision to the California Capitol, flipping the governor's seat red only a few years later. Donald Trump Donald Trump. Issue: February/March 2000 Trump claimed in March 2026 that Kennedy was a fan of his, touting that JFK Jr. even invited the real estate mogul to be on the cover of George. Others have claimed otherwise, attributing the decision to feature Trump as one that Kennedy's successor Frank Lalli made when he took over as editor-in-chief. "I wonder what John would have thought of all that,” Berman told Vanity Fair. “He missed so much."
